newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - OUB aims to be leading Asian bank.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OUB aims to be leading Asian bank.

text.p: Singapore's Overseas Union Bank (OUB) aims to become a leading Asian bank by expanding its corporate banking and fee-based operations, president and chief executive officer, Peter Seah, said on Friday.
Already the fifth largest bank in Southeast Asia, OUB is rapidly developing its non-Singaporean sources of income to help it overcome the limitations of its small domestic market.
"Our objective to be a leading regional bank," Seah told Reuters in an interview.
"OUB differentiates itself from the other Singapore banks in its spread of income. We are the only Singapore bank with more than 30 percent of our income derived from overseas operations."
Seah said OUB overseas income had grown from 20 percent about five years ago and the bank now aimed to increase its share over the next five years to at least 40 percent.
OUB turned in an impressive 22.3 percent profit rise year-on-year in the first half of calendar 1996 with a net of Singapore $142.15 million.
It currently ranks as Singapore's fourth largest bank, after The Development Bank of Singapore Ltd, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp and United Overseas Bank Ltd.

Within the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) -- which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- OUB lies fifth, behind Bangkok Bank, Seah said.
He said OUB had raised its capital funds from about S$900 million to S$3.0 billion over five years and would continue to grow to help it gain access to all fields of corporate banking.
Seah said he expected the bank to do well in 1996.
"I expect our second-half numbers in absolute terms to be better than the first half," he said.

He said the broad base of the bank's operations should help it overcome any slowdown in its domestic Singapore market, where growth might falter because of the recent slump in the city-state's core electronics market.

Singapore grew rapidly through the early 1990s with a jump of 8.8 percent in its gross domestic product (GDP) in 1995. But most analysts see GDP slipping in 1996 to between seven and eight percent and say 1997 may see a further slowdown.
Seah said he expected Singapore's economy to grow by six to seven percent in 1997.

"The economic slowdown in Singapore would probably translate into slower demand for credit. I think probably the area where the greatest impact will be would likely be the area of housing loans, particularly in the second half of 1997," Seah added.
He said the bank's corporate activities would continue to grow in several directions.
"At S$2.5 billion, our fund management portfolio is currently the highest among the Singapore banks."
He said it was already ASEAN's number one syndicating bank according to a report by the International Financial Review.

OUB was set to benefit from the growth of Singapore as a major financial and foreign exchange trading centre and already gained around 10 percent of its income from treasury operations, which include currency and commodity dealings, he said.
"Treasury operations have been growing and it is a significant percentage of our total bottom line," he said.
Seah said OUB's recent growth meant there was no pressing need to consider merger with another bank but it might consider raising further capital in future to strengthen its operations.
Asked if the bank could sell more shares through private placement in the future as it had done on three occasions in the past, Seah replied:
"As the need for capital continues, we have various options and one of them is to do private placements. I would say down the road, yes. I mean it is a question of when we do it."
